A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RLBR framework and Reward Bag Transformer research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: V2 reports original RBT and baseline evaluations on MuJoCo and DeepMind Control Suite tasks, together with component ablations, reward-reconstruction case studies and sensitivity experiments.

after.justification: V3 retains these original experiments and adds sparse-reward task results and further baseline comparisons.

M1.justification: The causal Transformer, bidirectional reward attention, next-state decoder, losses in Equations (4)–(7), and alternating reward-model/policy optimization remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 splits sampling and loss estimation into separate lines without changing the procedure.

E1.justification: V3 adds ball_in_cup-catch and reacher-hard evaluations with sparse success feedback in Table 2. The original eight control tasks and fixed-length, variable-length, trajectory-feedback and overlapping/gapped bag scenarios remain, making this a limited coverage extension.

E2.justification: V3 adds Random Network Distillation (RND) to the four-task MuJoCo comparison in Figure 6. Shaping matches v2's SAC-shaping, previously evaluated on Hopper and Walker2d, and now participates across the main fixed-bag comparisons. SAC, IRCR, RRD, LIRPG and HC remain evaluated.

E3.justification: V3 introduces a sparse-reward protocol using whole trajectories as single bags; Table 2 describes terminal binary success feedback. Existing bag configurations, 1000-step episode limits and training budgets remain unchanged. The relationship between this binary feedback, Appendix C's condition-based reward description and the reported evaluation scores is unclear.

E4.justification: The component ablation moves from v2 Appendix D.2/Figure 7 to v3 Section 5.3/Figure 5 with the same results. The overlapping/gapped-bag tests, Hopper reward-reconstruction case studies and sequence/relabel-length sensitivity analysis are also retained. The additional benchmark and baseline comparisons introduce no distinct ablation or diagnostic analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions already report means and standard deviations, six-seed main comparisons and ablations, three-run variable-length and architecture-sensitivity experiments, and paired t-tests at the 5% level for result tables. V3's added results follow these existing reporting practices.

E6.justification: New Table 2 reports RBT scores of 972.19 ± 5.50 on ball_in_cup-catch and 735.67 ± 144.90 on reacher-hard, versus Shaping's 847.88 ± 178.01 and 664.49 ± 170.50. V3 also adds Shaping and RND result curves. These are additional results; Table 1 and v2 Table 3/v3 Table 4 retain identical numerical entries.

T1.justification: V2 Definition 3.1 requires bag rewards to equal sums of latent immediate rewards. V3 removes that restriction from the definition and instead conditions its redistribution argument on preserving bag totals. Theorem 1 and Appendix B consequently concern equivalence with a redistributed-reward MDP rather than the original latent-reward MDP. Although the summation argument remains similar, the formal problem scope and guarantee are substantially redefined.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion reframe the theoretical contribution from connecting cumulative bagged rewards to the original MDP toward solving BRMDPs through properly redistributed rewards. Together with the introduction's more general bag-reward formulation, this changes the claimed scope of the central framework. The RBT architecture and broad empirical-superiority claims persist.

C2.justification: V3 adds interpretation of applicability to sparse-reward tasks and expands the explanation of why sparse-reward methods struggle with bagged feedback. It removes v2's sample-scarcity explanation for arbitrary-bag baseline failures, detailed shaping-noise interpretation, and conclusion discussion of sum-form aggregation limits and alternative aggregations.

D1.justification: Appendix C adds the sparse tasks' reward-trigger conditions and describes treating each trajectory as one reward bag. V2's explanation that shaping experiments used available task-specific weights for Hopper and Walker2d disappears. The RBT hyperparameters, training schedule, software, hardware and anonymous code-access link otherwise remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V3 adds reward-design references such as Kwon and Lee, and intrinsic-reward references including Burda, Sorg and Zheng et al. (2021). It removes the Transformers for RL discussion and associated works such as Kim's Preference Transformer. These revise supporting context and emphasis while retaining the main trajectory-feedback and reward-redistribution positioning.

P1.justification: The abstract, introductory motivation and related-work narrative receive substantial rewriting. The theoretical section moves into the reward-redistribution section, architecture and loss descriptions gain numbered subsections, and the experimental narrative is reorganized. Sparse-reward discussion moves into an expanded appendix, while the existing ablation moves into the main text.

P2.justification: V3 removes v2's reward-setting comparison schematic, redraws the architecture diagram, adds checkpoint annotations and a sparse-results table, and revises the baseline plots. The ablation moves into the main text with rescaled vertical axes. Figure 6 becomes a four-panel sparse-baseline comparison; its shared legend inconsistently maps Shaping and RBT colors across panels.

improvement.justification: Expanded baseline coverage and a more visible ablation are useful additions. However, the new sparse-reward evidence is difficult to interpret: Table 2 describes terminal 0/1 rewards but reports scores reaching 972.19 without clearly explaining the scoring distinction. V3 also removes the aggregation-limitations discussion while broadening the formulation, and Figure 6 introduces inconsistent color labeling. These benefits and reporting weaknesses prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
